subject: Dedicated capacity & GPU fleet modeling for Acme: throughput / SLO headroom
messages:
From: Lina Park <lina@acme.com>
To: marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-03-05T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Dedicated capacity planning for Acme Search — initial numbers

Marissa,

Thanks for the quick intro last week. To help us size a dedicated pool for our Acme Search phase-1 launch, here are the baseline numbers from infra/product: 

- Expected sustained peak: 450 qps (search API calls) during US morning ramp (1 hour window).
- Average client prompt tokens: ~220 tokens (user prompt + system context).
- Average generation length per request: ~180 tokens.
- Distribution: 70% short responses (<200 gen tokens), 20% medium (200-400), 10% long (>400).
- SLOs: 99th percentile end-to-end response time <= 800ms; cold-start 1st-token latency target not to exceed 300ms if possible.
- Canary requirement: we plan to start with a 10% traffic canary for 2 weeks, then ramp to 100% if metrics hold.

Can you and your infra team provide a capacity plan (GPUs required, expected tokens/sec per GPU, headroom, and estimated latency fit) and a recommended rollout? Also include an example of how we model burst headroom for a +30% traffic spike during events.

Thanks,
Lina Park
Head of Product — Acme Search
Acme Corp

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
To: Lina Park <lina@acme.com>
Cc: dev_patel@redwood.ai, karthik_iyer@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-03-05T10:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity planning for Acme Search — initial numbers

Lina — thanks for the detail. Looping in Dev (infra performance) and Karthik (dedicated ops) to produce a succinct capacity model and a recommended fleet plan and rollout.

Quick clarifying Qs before we run numbers:
- Is the 450 qps the absolute peak you need to sustain for the whole launch window, or an average across the hour (i.e., do you expect spikes beyond that inside the window)?
- Any hard requirement on model family / quantization? If you need the highest SRO/quality we’d pick an FP16 variant; if cost sensitivity is higher we can recommend quantized variants.

We’ll get a first-pass sizing + a spreadsheet with per-GPU tokens/sec numbers by model and recommended committed pool within 48 hours.

—Marissa
Sr. Account Exec, Redwood Inference

From: Dev Patel <dev_patel@redwood.ai>
To: marissa_cole@redwood.ai, karthik_iyer@redwood.ai
Cc: stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-03-06T08:30:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity planning for Acme Search — initial numbers

Marissa / Karthik — took Lina's numbers and did a draft throughput/latency model. Attachment: gpu_sizing_acme_q1_2026.xlsx (high-level). Key assumptions:

Assumptions (conservative):
- Model: "open-xxl-65b" FP16 serving profile (comparable to 65B-class).
- Avg tokens/request = prompt (220) + gen (180) = 400 tokens per request.
- Target SLO: P99 end-to-end <= 800ms. We'll break this into routing/ingress (50-100ms), model latency (remainder), and network tails.
- Use H100-class instance as baseline for latency-sensitive workloads; A100 80GB used as alternate (cost-sensitivity).

Measured throughputs (approx tokens/sec per GPU, mixed gen load, active KV cache):
- H100 (optimized kernels, batch size ~8): 12,500 tokens/sec per GPU (steady-state for generation-heavy mix)
- A100 80GB: 8,500 tokens/sec per GPU
- L4 / inference-optimized small accelerators: 3,000 tokens/sec per device (not recommended for this latency SLO at scale)

Raw compute math:
- Peak tokens/sec demand = QPS * avg tokens/request = 450 * 400 = 180,000 tokens/sec.
- GPUs needed (raw) = 180,000 / tokens_per_gpu
  - H100 raw = 180,000 / 12,500 = 14.4 GPUs
  - A100 raw = 180,000 / 8,500 = 21.2 GPUs

Operational headroom and SLO padding: we recommend a minimum of +20% sustained headroom to cover batching inefficiencies, KV misses, OS jitter, and background jobs. For burst resilience (+30% traffic spikes) we add an additional buffer or autoscale band.
- H100 recommended committed pool = ceil(14.4 * 1.2) = 18 GPUs
- A100 recommended committed pool = ceil(21.2 * 1.2) = 26 GPUs

SLO fit notes (latency):
- Under conservative per-GPU latency measurements, H100 baseline provides median generation latency for 180 tokens of ~120-160ms per request (model-only) assuming batching optimizations; end-to-end P99 we estimate ~350-500ms given intra-cluster variance, which fits the 800ms P99 requirement with safe headroom.
- A100 path likely increases model latency (median ~200-260ms) and P99 could approach the SLO boundary during sustained peak without extra headroom or vertical scaling.

Canary & rollout suggestion:
- Phase 1 (canary): Reserve 10% of traffic on 2 H100 nodes (equiv. to ~3-4 GPUs dedicated to canary) to validate latency metrics and tail behavior. Run for two weeks.
- Phase 2 (50%): Ramp to 50% with autoscale band (+15% burst capacity) and monitor P99/service_errors.
- Phase 3 (100%): Full pool (18 H100 GPUs) with autoscale to add up to +30% temporary capacity as needed.

Estimated cost delta & ops notes:
- H100 committed pool is more expensive but provides clear latency headroom and simpler rollout. A100 reduces compute costs but may push you close to P99 limits during sustained peaks—would require larger pool or tighter batching.

I attached a sample sheet that includes per-GPU qps mapping, cost per GPU-hour, and an example autoscale rule set. Happy to refine numbers if Acme can share: a 24-hour qps histogram (we only have the 1-hour peak) and typical prompt/gen token percentiles.

—Dev
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks Dev — this is exactly the level of detail we needed. Quick items: 

- We'll aim to provide a 24-hour qps histogram and sample traffic CSV (sending separately).
- Procurement note: Tom from procurement wants a committed monthly GPU count and a starter pricing estimate so he can draft the PO. Can you include a 12-month commitment vs month-to-month delta in the spreadsheet?

One follow-up on headroom: for the +30% spike you recommend autoscale. Can you describe how fast we can spin up extra capacity and what the expected cold-start tail would look like if we needed an emergency +30%? We need that for our ops runbook.

Best,
Lina

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
To: Lina Park <lina@acme.com>, Tom B. <tom.b@acme.com>
Cc: dev_patel@redwood.ai, karthik_iyer@redwood.ai, stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-03-08T15:42:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity planning for Acme Search — initial numbers

Lina / Tom — thanks. Per Dev's sheet attached, and answering the autoscale/cold-start Q: 

Autoscale & cold-start behavior (summary):
- Warm pool vs cold instances: our recommended committed pool (18 H100s) stays warm with loaded model shards and pre-warmed runtimes. Autoscaling beyond the committed pool provisions additional H100 instances from our dedicated capacity pool.
- Provision time: cold GPU instance provisioning to ready state (driver + model load) ~ 90-180 seconds depending on model size and quantization. We recommend a second short-lived warm buffer (2-3 kept-warm GPUs) for <60s spikes; autoscale fills the rest within the 90-180s window.
- Cold-start tails: during a rapid +30% surge that exceeds kept-warm buffer, the initial 90-180s will show higher p99 latency (potentially >1.5x) for requests routed to newly provisioned nodes. Strategy: route a small fraction of traffic to new nodes (gradual shift) and use query queuing for a brief window to prevent tail spikes.

Deliverables being shared:
- Attached: gpu_sizing_acme_q1_2026.xlsx (capacity math + 12-month committed vs month-to-month pricing bands)
- We'll also include a sample runbook snippet for autoscale thresholds and a recommended canary runbook.

Next steps: Dev / Karthik will update the spreadsheet with the 24-hour histogram once Acme sends it. Tom — if Procurement can share target budget bands, we can produce a matched committed offer.

Thanks — I’ve attached the redwood dedicated MOA draft for legal/procurement intake as well.

—Marissa
Sr. Account Exec, Redwood Inference
